Meta's gearing up for a stock sale.

On Monday, Meta launched a plan to raise up to $95 billion in stock, upsized Tuesday to $97.5 billion. Naturally, Nvidia and AMD, two of Meta's biggest chip suppliers, said they were buying. Nvidia would invest $3 billion and AMD $1 billion. Just 96% of the raise to go as the circle in circular finance continues to spin.

Meta carried about $115 billion in debt and lease obligations as of September 30, per its quarterly filing, within $206.45 billion in total liabilities. Its future commitments dwarf both. Bloomberg reported on October 22 that Meta's lease and contract commitments hit about $825 billion, up from nearly $700 billion in July. That total includes $355.7 billion in leases not yet on the balance sheet, per the filing. Nikkei Asia put the figure at $420 billion in late July.

Capex keeps climbing on top of that. Meta narrowed its 2026 guidance last week to $135 billion to $145 billion, raising the floor and implying $49 billion to $59 billion in Q4 spending alone. The combined weight likely forced Meta's hand: it issued more stock.

One stock. Nvidia-level potential. 30M+ investors trust Moby to find it first. Get the pick. Tap here.

At the same time, Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang said he would help Meta CEO Mark Zuckerberg out with $3 billion, the companies said. Meta plans to deploy more Nvidia Vera Rubin systems and Vera CPUs to support Muse, Meta's AI agent. Muse launched last month and is third on the U.S. free iPhone chart as of October 26, behind Vinted, a secondhand store app, and TikTok Pro. It's ahead of ChatGPT, Claude, and Gemini.

The good thing about issuing new common shares is Meta doesn't have to pay anything back or pay interest. That said, $12.5 billion of preferred pays a 6.5% dividend. The bad thing is shareholders get diluted by about 5.5% if the full plan sells, per a StockTitan estimate. EPS is also going to take a hit if Meta can't pump its profits.

But that's the price Big Tech and the hyperscalers feel is worth paying to guarantee their slice of the AI industry. If they don't grab it now, someone else will.

Tech stocks were higher late Wednesday afternoon with the State Street Technology Select Sector SPDR ETF (XLK) rising 0.6% and the State Street SPDR S&P Semiconductor ETF (XSD) up 0.4%.

The Philadelphia Semiconductor Index advanced 1.5%.

In corporate news, Oracle (ORCL) shares rose more than 11% after it reaffirmed its fiscal 2027 outlook and set long-term targets at its Investor Day on Wednesday, including FY30 revenue of $225 billion or more.

The US Department of Justice is examining how Nvidia's (NVDA) planned $12.93 billion acquisition of Hugging Face could affect competition in the AI sector, Reuters reported. Nvidia shares were down 1.5%.

OpenAI is planning to buy AI computing chips from Alphabet's (GOOGL) Google to help build its infrastructure, The Information reported. Alphabet shares rose 1.3%.

Dropbox (DBX) is cutting about 9% of its global workforce. The company estimates the reduction will result in cash expenditures of $27 million to $33 million, primarily for severance payments, employee benefits and related costs. The company's shares fell 1.3%.

title: SK Hynix Just Delivered Great News for Micron Investors

It would be odd to say that investors are too pessimistic about a stock that has tripled this year, but that appears to be the case for Micron (NASDAQ:MU).

Shares of the leading memory chipmaker are up 240% this year, but they're down more than 20% since peaking after Micron's fiscal third-quarter earnings report.

Missed Nvidia in 2009? This Rare Signal Is Flashing Again. In 2009, a "Double Down" signal flashed for a little-known chipmaker called Nvidia. For the first time in years, that same "Total Conviction" signal is flashing for a company 1/100th the size of Nvidia. Continue »

In the months since, investors have hotly debated the sustainability of the memory chip boom, driven by a shortage that has led to sky-high prices. Even as supply-and-demand conditions have tightened since June, investors seem to believe that Micron stock has peaked and that they're better off hedging their bets in anticipation of the cycle's downside.

However, one of the other big three chip companies just reported earnings, and the results and commentary continue to support an extended shortage of memory chips, as Hynix said it expected demand to outpace supply through 2030. Additionally, the company said it was virtually sold out through 2029.

Image source: The Motley Fool.

What the Hynix report showed

Like Micron before it, SK Hynix (NASDAQ:SKHY) reported blockbuster results in its third quarter, with revenue up 328% year-over-year and 32% sequentially, showing that the tailwinds in the industry remain strong even from the previous quarter.

Importantly, prices are still going up as the company reported a high 20% sequential increase in average selling prices (ASP) for DRAM chips, which includes the high bandwidth memory (HBM) deployed at AI data centers, and it had mid-20% sequential growth in NAND, which is typically used for data storage.

Hynix also reported 10% sequential DRAM bit growth, a solid increase in volume, while NAND was down slightly.

The company also made a number of predictions beyond demand exceeding supply through 2030, which Micron investors will want to hear.

Management predicted that the global AI data center infrastructure market will expand by 40% annually through 2030, indicating it would quadruple in four years. It also said that memory demand would exceed earlier expectations as AI takes on longer, more complex tasks, driving a surge in compute and data processing.

At the enterprise level, it said that personal AI would drive near-term growth, while physical AI would broaden the scope of demand over the mid- to long-term.
